summary.text: An ice shelf is a large, thick platform of glacial ice that floats on the ocean, fed by one or more glaciers flowing off the land.
Pressure from the grounded ice, driven by gravity, keeps pushing ice from the grounding line out to the seaward front, where masses of ice break away in calving events.
Ice shelves act as brakes on the glaciers behind them, and once a shelf is gone those glaciers speed up and may dump more ice into the ocean than they gain as snow.

items.prompt: The floating shelf at the end of an Antarctic glacier breaks apart and disappears. What tends to happen to the glacier behind it?

options.label: It slows down and thickens
It speeds up toward the sea
It stops moving altogether
It starts flowing back inland

items.explain: Shelves act as brakes; when they are removed, the glaciers feeding them increase in speed, as already seen on the Antarctic Peninsula.

items.prompt: Roughly how much of a floating shelf of glacier ice sits above the sea surface?

options.label: Almost none of it
About half of it
About three-quarters
At least about one-ninth

items.explain: Because glacial ice is less dense than seawater, at least 1/9 of the floating ice stands above the surface.

items.prompt: In a steady state, how do Antarctica's ice shelves lose their mass?

options.label: About half melts from below, half breaks off
Nearly all of it melts at the surface in summer
Nearly all of it is blown away as snow
All of it breaks off as icebergs

items.explain: About half is lost to basal melt and half to calving, though the balance varies from shelf to shelf.

items.prompt: A ship's crew finds a flat sheet of ice about 1 m thick that froze on the sea surface this winter. Is it an ice shelf?

options.label: Yes, because it is flat and floating
Yes, because it lies along a coast

items.explain: Sea ice forms on water and is usually under 3 m thick, while an ice shelf is thick glacier ice that flows off the land.

items.prompt: What mainly drives a floating ice shelf to keep moving out to sea?

options.label: Ocean currents dragging its underside
Gravity-driven push from ice resting on land
Strong winds blowing across its surface
Tides lifting and pulling it each day

items.explain: Pressure from the grounded ice, caused by gravity, moves ice from the grounding line to the seaward front.

items.prompt: A glacier flows off the coast into ever deeper water. Why does it lift off the seabed and start to float?

options.label: Air bubbles make it lighter than fresh water
Tides push it up from underneath

items.explain: Shelves form where the ice is not thick enough to displace the denser ocean water around it, so it floats.

paragraphs.heading: A floating plate of glacier ice
paragraphs.text: An ice shelf is a huge, thick platform of glacier ice that floats on the ocean. One or more glaciers flowing off the land feed it, so new ice keeps arriving. Ice shelves are found in Antarctica and in the Arctic, in Greenland, northern Canada and the Russian Arctic. They are roughly 100 to 1,000 m thick. The two largest are both in Antarctica: the Ross and the Filchner-Ronne.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same as sea ice
paragraphs.text: An ice shelf is different from sea ice. Sea ice forms by freezing on the water, is much thinner, usually under 3 m, and covers parts of the Arctic Ocean and the Southern Ocean around Antarctica. An ice shelf starts as ice from the land and begins to float along coasts where it is no longer thick enough to push aside the denser seawater around it. The line where floating ice meets ice resting on rock or sediment is called the grounding line. The seaward edge, facing the open ocean, is the ice front or calving front.

paragraphs.heading: Always on the move
paragraphs.text: Ice shelves keep moving. Gravity makes the grounded ice behind them press outward, and that pressure carries ice steadily from the grounding line to the front. The front usually creeps forward for years or decades until a major calving event, when a large mass of ice suddenly breaks away. Snow piling up on top and melting from underneath also matter for how much ice a shelf holds. New ice can also freeze onto its underside.

paragraphs.heading: How high it floats
paragraphs.text: Glacier ice is less dense than seawater, so part of a floating shelf always rises above the waves. At least 1/9 of it sits above the surface, and the exact share depends on how much squeezed air is trapped in bubbles left over from compressed snow. Cold seawater has a density of about 1028 kg/m³, while glacier ice ranges from about 850 kg/m³ up toward 920 kg/m³, the figure for very cold ice with no bubbles. Lighter snow lying on top of the glacier ice can lift the shelf even higher.

paragraphs.heading: Brakes on the glaciers
paragraphs.text: Ice shelves act as brakes on the glaciers that feed them. They also limit how much melting happens on the surfaces of those glaciers. When a shelf is lost, its glaciers speed up, because meltwater seeps in, because less is holding them back, or both. They may then pour more ice into the ocean than they collect as snow. This speed-up has already been seen in places where shelves fell apart in earlier years.

paragraphs.heading: Shelves in retreat
paragraphs.text: Over the last several decades, glacier scientists have watched ice shelves shrink through melting, calving and, for some, complete break-up. In recent decades Antarctica's shelves have lost more ice to melting from below and to calving than new ice and snow have replaced. Two parts of the Larsen Ice Shelf shattered into hundreds of small pieces in 1995 and 2002, and Larsen C let go a huge ice island in 2017. The Prince Gustav Ice Shelf shrank from 1,600 km² to 1,100 km² by 2008. The Ayles shelf fell apart in 2005 and the Markham shelf in 2008, and the Milne Ice Shelf broke off in August 2020.
